claim: The crystal structure of the CTD-SP1 Gag fragment is a goblet-shaped hexamer in which the cup comprises the CTD and an ensuing type II β-turn, and the stem comprises a 6-helix bundle.
source: The crystal structure of the CTD-SP1 Gag fragment is a goblet-shaped hexamer in which the cup comprises the CTD and an ensuing type II β-turn, and the stem comprises a 6-helix bundle.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript, including structural coordinates and electron density maps.

claim: The β-turn is critical for immature virus assembly.
source: The β-turn is critical for immature virus assembly and the 6-helix bundle regulates proteolysis during maturation.
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis experiments showing that β-turn mutations disrupt assembly, and by structural analysis showing the β-turn's role in organizing hexamer-stabilizing elements.

claim: The 6-helix bundle regulates proteolysis during maturation.
source: The β-turn is critical for immature virus assembly and the 6-helix bundle regulates proteolysis during maturation.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data showing the scissile bond is sequestered within the 6-helix bundle, and by inference about the need for unfolding to allow protease access.

claim: HIV-1 maturation inhibitors suppress unfolding of the CA-SP1 junction and thereby delay access of the viral protease to its substrate.
source: Our results also indicate that HIV-1 maturation inhibitors suppress unfolding of the CA-SP1 junction and thereby delay access of the viral protease to its substrate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural data showing the 6-helix bundle sequesters the scissile bond, combined with knowledge about maturation inhibitor function.

claim: During assembly, Gag makes a spherical, immature capsid shell that packages the viral genome, directs interactions with the plasma membrane to promote envelopment, and recruits cellular machinery to release the new virus particle from the host cell.
source: During assembly, Gag makes a spherical, immature capsid shell that packages the viral genome, directs interactions with the plasma membrane to promote envelopment, and recruits cellular machinery to release the new virus particle from the host cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 assembly that is cited in the introduction.

claim: The Gag shell has hexagonal paracrystalline lattice symmetry, wherein the central CA region makes two layers of interactions through its two domains (NTD and CTD).
source: The Gag shell has hexagonal paracrystalline lattice symmetry, wherein the central CA region makes two layers of interactions through its two domains (NTD and CTD, for N-terminal and C-terminal domain).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the immature Gag lattice structure.

claim: During maturation, Gag is cleaved by the viral protease at specific sites, resulting in disassembly of the Gag shell and release of new structural proteins, which then rearrange into the mature, infectious virion.
source: During maturation, Gag is cleaved by the viral protease at specific sites. This results in disassembly of the Gag shell and release of new structural proteins, which then rearrange into the mature, infectious virion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 maturation.

claim: In the mature virion, the genome is repackaged inside a cone-shaped capsid made up of the CA protein, with the NTD forming hexameric or pentameric rings that are connected by the CTD.
source: In the mature virion, the genome is repackaged inside a cone-shaped capsid made up of the CA protein, with the NTD forming hexameric or pentameric rings that are connected by the CTD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mature HIV-1 capsid structure.

claim: The MA-CA junction is in an extended configuration in the immature virion.
source: One switch spans the MA-CA junction, which is in an extended configuration in the immature virion (Kelly et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Upon proteolysis, the new CA N-terminus folds into a β-hairpin stabilized by a buried salt bridge between the new N-terminal proline and a conserved aspartate residue and promotes assembly of the mature capsid.
source: Upon proteolysis, the new CA N-terminus folds into a β-hairpin stabilized by a buried salt bridge between the new N-terminal proline and a conserved aspartate residue and promotes assembly of the mature capsid (Gitti et al., 1996; von Schwedler et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous structural and functional studies.

claim: The CA-SP1 junction is predicted to fold into an α-helix.
source: The CA-SP1 junction is predicted to fold into an α-helix (Accola et al., 1998; Liang et al., 2002), and forms the binding site of so-called 'maturation inhibitors,' as exemplified by 3-O-(3',3'-dimethylsuccinyl)betulinic acid (bevirimat) (reviewed in Adamson et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CA-SP1 junction forms the binding site of maturation inhibitors such as bevirimat.
source: The CA-SP1 junction is predicted to fold into an α-helix (Accola et al., 1998; Liang et al., 2002), and forms the binding site of so-called 'maturation inhibitors,' as exemplified by 3-O-(3',3'-dimethylsuccinyl)betulinic acid (bevirimat) (reviewed in Adamson et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Maturation inhibitors delay proteolysis of the CA-SP1 junction and induce aberrant maturation.
source: These inhibitors delay proteolysis of the CA-SP1 junction and induce aberrant maturation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about maturation inhibitor function.

claim: The importance of the CA-SP1 junction as a regulator of proteolysis during maturation is well established.
source: The importance of the CA-SP1 junction as a regulator of proteolysis during maturation is well established (Kräusslich et al., 1995; Pettit et al., 1994; Wiegers et al., 1998), but the molecular basis of this function has been unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CA-SP1 junction is important for assembly of the immature HIV-1 Gag shell.
source: Mutagenesis studies also indicate that the CA-SP1 junction is important for assembly of the immature HIV-1 Gag shell (Accola et al., 1998; Al-Mawsawi et al., 2014; Datta et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2005; Kräusslich et al., 1995; Liang et al., 2002; Liang et al., 2003; Melamed et al., 2004; Pettit et al., 1994; Rihn et al., 2013; von Schwedler et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple mutagenesis studies.

claim: Low resolution electron microscopy studies indicate that the CA-SP1 junction forms what appears to be a pillar of density or helical bundle.
source: Low resolution electron microscopy studies indicate that the junction forms what appears to be a pillar of density or helical bundle, and so is likely to stabilize the Gag lattice (Schur et al., 2015a; Schur et al., 2015b; Wright et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous electron microscopy studies.

claim: Neither the SP1 spacer nor the putative helical bundle is a universal feature of retroviral Gag shells.
source: However, neither the SP1 spacer nor the putative helical bundle is a universal feature of retroviral Gag shells (Bharat et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a comparative structural study.

claim: Structural studies of the HIV-1 CA-SP1 junction in context of longer Gag fragments (CTD-SP1 and CTD-SP1-NC) have shown that the junction is primarily disordered.
source: Structural studies of the HIV-1 CA-SP1 junction in context of longer Gag fragments (CTD-SP1 and CTD-SP1-NC) have shown that the junction is primarily disordered (Newman et al., 2004; Worthylake et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous NMR studies.

claim: The backbone NMR chemical shifts of CA-SP1 junction residues deviate from expected random coil values, indicating a small propensity towards an α-helical conformation.
source: Nevertheless, the backbone NMR chemical shifts of junction residues deviate from expected random coil values, indicating a small propensity towards an α-helical conformation (Newman et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an NMR study.

claim: The isolated SP1 peptide displays concentration dependent secondary structure in aqueous solution, and folds into an α-helix at the millimolar protein concentrations found in virions.
source: Indeed, the isolated SP1 peptide displays concentration dependent secondary structure in aqueous solution, and folds into an α-helix at the millimolar protein concentrations found in virions (Datta et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a biophysical study.

claim: Nucleic acids (both RNA and DNA) can promote Gag assembly in vitro, presumably because of proximity-induced interactions between multiple copies of Gag that bind to the same nucleic acid molecule.
source: Nucleic acids (both RNA and DNA) can promote Gag assembly in vitro, presumably because of proximity-induced interactions between multiple copies of Gag that bind to the same nucleic acid molecule (Campbell and Rein, 1999; Campbell and Vogt, 1995; Gross et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous in vitro assembly studies, with a speculative explanation.

claim: The CTD-SP1 fragment of HIV-1 Gag contains the minimal information required to assemble the immature lattice, whereas the NTD is dispensable.
source: The CTD-SP1 fragment of HIV-1 Gag contains the minimal information required to assemble the immature lattice, whereas the NTD is dispensable (Accola et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Purified CTD-SP1 protein assembled in vitro into flat sheets with the subunits organized into a hexagonal lattice with the expected unit cell spacing of the CTD layer of the immature Gag lattice (~74 Å).
source: Accordingly, we found that purified CTD-SP1 protein assembled in vitro into flat sheets with the subunits organized into a hexagonal lattice with the expected unit cell spacing of the CTD layer of the immature Gag lattice (~74 Å) (Wright et al., 2007 ) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 2D crystallography shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and comparison to a cited reference.

claim: The crystal structure was determined to R/Rfree values of 0.246/0.278.
source: Diffraction data were collected from a single crystal at beamline 22-ID at the Advanced Photon Source, and processed with HKL2000 (Otwinowski and Minor, 1997). The phase problem was solved by molecular replacement with an immature CTD hexamer model (PDB 4USN) (Schur et al., 2015b). Upon rigid body refinement, unbiased densities for the 6-helix bundle were readily observed in model-phased maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). Multiple rounds of iterative model building and refinement were performed with the programs PHENIX (version 1.9–1692) (Adams et al., 2010) and Coot (Emsley et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: The entire CTD-SP1 hexamer gave an excellent fit to an 8.8 Å resolution cryoEM map of the immature HIV-1 Gag lattice.
source: The entire CTD-SP1 hexamer – including both the main CTD fold and ordered SP1 residues – gave an excellent fit to an 8.8 Å resolution cryoEM map of the immature HIV-1 Gag lattice (Schur et al., 2015b) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fitting analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and comparison to a cited cryoEM structure.

claim: The CTD-SP1 plate crystals were made up of stacked sheets of flat hexagonal lattices, with each sheet consisting of CTD-SP1 hexamers connected by CTD dimer linkages.
source: The CTD-SP1 plate crystals were made up of stacked sheets of flat hexagonal lattices, with each sheet consisting of CTD-SP1 hexamers connected by CTD dimer linkages (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The crystal structure represents a flattened version of the immature HIV-1 Gag lattice.
source: Our structure therefore represents a flattened version of the immature HIV-1 Gag lattice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of the crystal structure to the curved cryoEM structure.

claim: Generation of Gag curvature does not necessarily require the kinds of conformational variations observed in the mature capsid subunits.
source: It therefore seems that generation of Gag curvature does not necessarily require the kinds of conformational variations observed in the mature capsid subunits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that flattening of the lattice results in minimal structural changes.

claim: Each CTD-SP1 subunit contains the main CTD fold (amino acids 281–351) and the CA-SP1 switch region (residues 352–370).
source: In our crystal structure, each subunit contains the main CTD fold (amino acids 281–351 in the HIV-1 Gag numbering scheme) and the CA-SP1 switch region (residues 352–370).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The CTD adopts the canonical fold: a short 310 helix, followed by a strand/turn element called the major homology region (MHR), and then four α-helices (helices 8–11).
source: The CTD adopts the canonical fold: a short 310 helix, followed by a strand/turn element called the major homology region (MHR), and then four α-helices (helices 8–11) (Gamble et al., 1997; Worthylake et al., 1999) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 2A and citations to previous structures.

claim: The CA-SP1 switch region consists of two parts: a type II β-turn (residues 352–355) and an α-helix that spans the CA-SP1 junction (residues 356–370).
source: The switch region immediately follows the main CTD fold, and consists of two parts: a type II β-turn (residues 352–355) and an α-helix that spans the CA-SP1 junction (residues 356–370).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The bipartite character of the CA-SP1 switch region could explain the apparent structural variability in the C-terminal switch regions of immature retroviral capsids.
source: This bipartite character was not anticipated but could explain the apparent structural variability in the C-terminal switch regions of immature retroviral capsids, which were discerned from subnanometer resolution cryoEM maps (Bharat et al., 2012; Schur et al., 2015a; 2015b).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the structure and comparison to cited cryoEM studies.

claim: Comparison of the immature CTD-SP1 subunit with the mature CTD subunit reveals a local conformational change (presence or absence of a kink) in the dimerization helix.
source: Comparison of the immature CTD-SP1 subunit with the mature CTD subunit reveals a local conformational change (presence or absence of a kink) in the dimerization helix, as noted previously (Bartonova et al., 2008) (arrows in Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2A,B and citation to a previous study.

claim: In the mature CTD, residues downstream of helix 11 are disordered.
source: Another difference is that, in the mature CTD, residues downstream of helix 11 are disordered (Bartonova et al., 2008; Gamble et al., 1997; Worthylake et al., 1999) (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies and shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The C-terminal tail of CA becomes unfolded upon maturation and has no apparent role in assembly of the mature capsid.
source: These observations provide further support for the presumption that the C-terminal tail of CA becomes unfolded upon maturation and has no apparent role in assembly of the mature capsid.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural comparison showing disorder in the mature form.

claim: The CTD-SP1 hexamer looks like a goblet, with the main CTD fold forming the cup and the CA-SP1 junction forming the stem.
source: The CTD-SP1 hexamer looks like a goblet, with the main CTD fold forming the cup and the CA-SP1 junction forming the stem (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Lateral packing between the CTD-SP1 subunits is quite loose along the body of the cup, and close contacts involving the main CTD fold occur only where the cup meets the stem.
source: Lateral packing between the subunits is quite loose along the body of the cup, and close contacts involving the main CTD fold occur only where the cup meets the stem.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The junction helices form a 6-helix bundle as predicted.
source: Underneath the cup, the junction helices form a 6-helix bundle as predicted (Accola et al., 1998; Wright et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure data and citations to previous predictions.

claim: All of the aliphatic sidechains in the junction helix make 'knobs-in-holes' interactions similar to classical coiled-coils.
source: All of the aliphatic sidechains in the junction helix make 'knobs-in-holes' interactions similar to classical coiled-coils (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: During HIV-1 maturation, the CA-SP1 junction is one of ten cleavage sites in the precursor Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins that are cleaved by the viral protease.
source: During HIV-1 maturation, the CA-SP1 junction is one of ten cleavage sites in the precursor Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins that are cleaved by the viral protease (PR).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV-1 maturation.

claim: Proteolytic processing occurs at different rates, with the CTD-SP1 junction processed with the slowest rate, and the downstream SP1-NC junction the fastest.
source: Proteolytic processing occurs at different rates, with the CTD-SP1 junction processed with the slowest rate, and the downstream SP1-NC junction the fastest (reviewed in Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The C-terminal boundary of the junction helix tracks precisely with sequence conservation; downstream residues that are disordered in the crystal structure are not conserved.
source: The C-terminal boundary of the junction helix tracks precisely with sequence conservation; downstream residues that are disordered in our crystal structure are not conserved (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2C and the crystal structure.

claim: The downstream SP1-NC junction has the fastest rate of processing because it is disordered in the immature virion.
source: This is consistent with the notion that the downstream SP1-NC junction has the fastest rate of processing because it is disordered in the immature virion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between disorder and processing rate.

claim: In the CTD-SP1 structure, the scissile bond (between Leu363 and Ala364) is located inside the helical barrel, where it is sequestered within a pocket covered by a methionine sidechain (Met367).
source: In our structure, the scissile bond (between Leu363 and Ala364) is located inside the helical barrel (yellow spheres in Figure 3A), where it is sequestered within a pocket covered by a methionine sidechain (Met367) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3A and 3D.

claim: When the CA-SP1 junction binds to PR, it adopts a fully extended, β-strand configuration wherein sidechains on either side of the scissile bond occupy sub-pockets within the enzyme active site.
source: When the CA-SP1 junction binds to PR, it adopts a fully extended, β-strand configuration wherein sidechains on either side of the scissile bond occupy sub-pockets within the enzyme active site (Prabu-Jeyabalan et al., 2000) (Figure 3E, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous structure and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the CTD-SP1 hexamer, the sidechains that occupy PR sub-pockets mediate the 'knobs-in-holes' interactions of the 6-helix bundle.
source: In the CTD-SP1 hexamer, these same sidechains mediate the 'knobs-in-holes' interactions of the 6-helix bundle (Figure 3E, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3E.

claim: For PR to gain access to its substrate, the 6-helix bundle must unfold.
source: Therefore, for PR to gain access to its substrate, the 6-helix bundle must unfold.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural observation that the scissile bond is sequestered in the bundle.

claim: The rate limiting step for proteolysis at the CA-SP1 site is unfolding of the 6-helix bundle.
source: Since proteolysis rates for the different cleavage sites are comparable when measured with peptide substrates (Lee et al., 2012), the rate limiting step for the CA-SP1 site is unfolding of the 6-helix bundle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural data and cited kinetic data.

claim: The CA-SP1 junction displays the slowest rate of proteolysis and is the final trigger that elicits HIV-1 maturation.
source: This explains why the CA-SP1 junction displays the slowest rate of proteolysis and is the final trigger that elicits HIV-1 maturation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural and kinetic data.

claim: The β-turn motif (352GVGGP356) makes a right-handed type II β-turn that buries the Val353 sidechain within a shallow sub-pocket at the bottom of the CTD.
source: This motif makes a right-handed type II β-turn that buries the Val353 sidechain within a shallow sub-pocket at the bottom of the CTD, which is made of the MHR and 9/10 loops.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In context of the hexamer, the entire β-turn is almost completely buried within a larger pocket made up of two MHR loops, two 9/10 loops, and the junction helices from three adjacent subunits.
source: In context of the hexamer, the entire β-turn is almost completely buried within a larger pocket made up of two MHR loops, two 9/10 loops, and the junction helices from three adjacent subunits (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The β-turn brings together multiple structural elements to generate the Gag hexamer.
source: Thus, the β-turn brings together multiple structural elements to generate the Gag hexamer.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural observation of the β-turn's interactions.

claim: The β-turn is a critical Gag assembly determinant.
source: This key structural role indicates that the β-turn is a critical Gag assembly determinant.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural role of the β-turn.

claim: Virtually all of the 19 single-point mutations in the structured region of the CA-SP1 switch (residues 352–370) resulted in aberrantly assembled particles and/or protein aggregates.
source: In contrast, virtually all of the 19 single-point mutations in the structured region of the CA-SP1 switch (residues 352–370) resulted in aberrantly assembled particles and/or protein aggregates (Figure 5A, Table 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 5, Table 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many of the CA-SP1 switch mutants appeared to behave in an 'all-or-none' manner, indicating that both the β-turn and junction helix must be functional for assembly to occur in vitro.
source: Apart from residues close to the C-terminal end of the junction helix, many of the switch mutants appeared to behave in an 'all-or-none' manner (i.e., they either assembled immature VLPs or aberrantly), indicating that both the β-turn and junction helix must be functional for assembly to occur in vitro.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The 'all-or-none' behavior of CA-SP1 switch mutants must be due to a defect in nucleation.
source: Such a behavior was unexpected because in high-order assembly systems, local defects in protein-protein interactions are typically buffered by cooperativity. Therefore, the 'all-or-none' behavior must be due to a defect in nucleation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mutagenesis data and knowledge of assembly systems.

claim: In the presence of tartrate, most of the CA-SP1 switch mutants failed to form immature VLPs, but instead assembled efficiently into thin-walled mature-like particles.
source: In this format, most of the CA-SP1 switch mutants again failed to form immature VLPs, but now instead assembled efficiently into thin-walled mature-like particles (Figure 5E–H, Table 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 5E–H, Table 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nucleation of the immature particles requires folding of both the β-turn and junction helix.
source: Since junction residues downstream of the main CTD fold are not required for assembly of the mature lattice and are almost certainly unfolded in the thin-walled particles, these results further indicate that nucleation of the immature particles requires folding of both the β-turn and junction helix.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mutagenesis data comparing immature and mature assembly.

claim: The identity of the particle (immature-like or mature-like) is established at nucleation.
source: We believe that this is an important observation, because it indicates that the identity of the particle is established at nucleation (Gross et al., 2000), and is more supportive of a disassembly/reassembly pathway of HIV-1 capsid maturation than a displacive or condensation mechanism (Keller et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that particles are either immature or mature, not mixed, and supported by citations.

claim: Although the HIV-1 Gag protein does not require nucleic acid to assemble into immature particles in vitro, folding of the CA-SP1 switch can be promoted by nucleic acid, likely due to clustering.
source: These results indicate that, although the HIV-1 Gag protein does not require nucleic acid to assemble into immature particles in vitro, folding of the CA-SP1 switch can be promoted by nucleic acid, likely due to clustering.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential behavior of mutants in DNA vs. tartrate assembly conditions.

claim: Mutations at the MHR loop (P289A, K290A) and the 9/10 loop (P328A, D329A) that surround the Val353 pocket behaved similarly to the β-turn and junction helix mutations.
source: Finally, we tested mutations at the MHR loop (P289A, K290A) and the 9/10 loop (P328A, D329A) that surround the Val353 pocket at the bottom of the CTD. These mutants behaved in a similar way as the β-turn and junction helix mutations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Table 2.

claim: Binding of Val353 to the bottom of the CTD, and proper folding of the β-turn, is a critical step in nucleation of the immature VLPs.
source: These results confirm that binding of Val353 to the bottom of the CTD – and by inference, proper folding of the β-turn – is a critical step in nucleation of the immature VLPs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The valine pocket at the bottom of the CTD functions as a folding chamber or 'chaperone' for the β-turn.
source: We speculate that the valine pocket at the bottom of the CTD functions as a folding chamber or 'chaperone' for the β-turn.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: The crystal structure of CTD-SP1 confirms prediction that the CA-SP1 junction forms a 6-helix bundle to sequester the PR cleavage site.
source: Our crystal structure of CTD-SP1 represents the highest resolution structure of the immature HIV-1 Gag lattice to date, and confirms prediction that the CA-SP1 junction forms a 6-helix bundle to sequester the PR cleavage site.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure data and comparison to previous predictions.

claim: The CA-SP1 junction elicits the slowest rate of proteolysis during maturation because the 6-helix bundle must unfold to bind PR.
source: The CA-SP1 junction elicits the slowest rate of proteolysis during maturation because the 6-helix bundle must unfold to bind PR.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural data showing sequestration of the scissile bond.

claim: PR gains substrate access by transient, cooperative unfolding and refolding of the 6-helix bundle.
source: Another attractive possibility is that PR gains substrate access by transient, cooperative unfolding and refolding of the 6-helix bundle (Bush and Vogt, 2014).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and citation.

claim: The proposed mechanism for PR access is analogous to the predicted transient unfolding of the collagen triple helix that permits cleavage by matrix metalloproteases.
source: Our proposed mechanism is analogous to the predicted transient unfolding of the collagen triple helix that permits cleavage by matrix metalloproteases (Lu and Stultz, 2013).
evidence: The claim draws an analogy to a cited mechanism in another system.

claim: Maturation inhibitors like bevirimat deny PR access by stabilizing the 6-helix bundle and inhibiting its unfolding.
source: Our analysis also supports a model wherein maturation inhibitors like bevirimat deny PR access, not by sequestering the scissile bond (the 6-helix bundle already does this), but rather by stabilizing the 6-helix bundle and inhibiting its unfolding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural data and knowledge of maturation inhibitor function.

claim: Resistance to maturation inhibitors can develop by means of mutations that destabilize the junction helix.
source: This model predicts that resistance can develop by means of mutations that destabilize the junction. Such mutations would enhance proteolysis in the absence of the maturation inhibitor, and indeed this seems to be a general property of well-characterized escape mutations (Adamson et al., 2006; Li et al., 2006; Sakalian et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural model and supported by citations to resistance studies.

claim: Some escape mutations that have been selected for in tissue culture appear to destabilize the Gag hexamer altogether, and the mutant viruses become dependent on the inhibitor to assemble.
source: In fact, some escape mutations that have been selected for in tissue culture appear to destabilize the Gag hexamer altogether, and the mutant viruses become dependent on the inhibitor to assemble (Waki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The T371I mutation stabilizes the 6-helix bundle and inhibits proteolysis even in the absence of inhibitor.
source: Conversely, mutations that stabilize the 6-helix bundle would be expected to inhibit proteolysis even in the absence of inhibitor. One such mutation is T371I (Fontana et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural model and supported by citation.

claim: The isoleucine substitution at position 371 stabilizes and extends the junction helix.
source: This residue immediately follows the junction helix, and we speculate that the isoleucine substitution stabilizes and extends the helix.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on structural reasoning.

claim: Bevirimat has been crosslinked to both the junction helix and the MHR.
source: We have not yet been able to determine whether bevirimat binds outside or inside the bundle, but the compound has been crosslinked to both the junction helix and the MHR (Nguyen et al., 2011), which seems consistent with the second possibility.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a crosslinking study.

claim: The β-turn is almost completely buried within an assembly-induced pocket surrounded by three adjacent subunits.
source: The β-turn is almost completely buried within an assembly-induced pocket surrounded by three adjacent subunits.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure.

claim: The β-turn interacts with 7 other hexamer-stabilizing structural elements.
source: Both its location and the fact that it interacts with 7 other hexamer-stabilizing structural elements indicate that the β-turn is a critical Gag assembly determinant, and may act as a 'clasp' that locks the interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The β-turn may act as a 'clasp' that locks the hexamer interactions.
source: Both its location and the fact that it interacts with 7 other hexamer-stabilizing structural elements indicate that the β-turn is a critical Gag assembly determinant, and may act as a 'clasp' that locks the interactions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the structural data.

claim: Assembly defects in the CA-SP1 switch region were graded, with the most severe mutations mapping to the β-turn and severity falling off towards the C-terminus of the junction helix.
source: Although our in vitro assembly experiments indicated that virtually the entire CA-SP1 switch region is intolerant of mutations, we did observe that assembly defects were graded – the most severe mutations mapped to the β-turn and severity fell off towards the C-terminus of the junction helix (i.e., the SP1 spacer).
evidence: The claim is supported by the mutagenesis data.

claim: A similar trend in assembly defect severity has been observed in previous studies, and the gradation is significantly more pronounced in cells.
source: A similar trend has been observed in previous studies, and indeed, the gradation in assembly defect is significantly more pronounced in cells (Accola et al., 1998; Al-Mawsawi et al., 2014; Datta et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2005; Kräusslich et al., 1995; Liang et al., 2002; Liang et al., 2003; Melamed et al., 2004; Rihn et al., 2013; von Schwedler et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous mutagenesis studies.

claim: HIV-1 Gag that completely lacks the SP1 spacer can still assemble into large, membrane-associated patches.
source: For example, HIV-1 Gag that completely lacks the SP1 spacer can still assemble into large, membrane-associated patches (Kräusslich et al., 1995), whereas β-turn mutants do not form plasma membrane-associated patches and remain diffusely distributed throughout the cytosol (Liang et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: β-turn mutants do not form plasma membrane-associated patches and remain diffusely distributed throughout the cytosol.
source: For example, HIV-1 Gag that completely lacks the SP1 spacer can still assemble into large, membrane-associated patches (Kräusslich et al., 1995), whereas β-turn mutants do not form plasma membrane-associated patches and remain diffusely distributed throughout the cytosol (Liang et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: SP1 is not strictly required for the fundamental higher-order self-association property of HIV-1 Gag.
source: These observations indicate that SP1 is not strictly required for the fundamental higher-order self-association property of HIV-1 Gag.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Gag lacking SP1 can still form membrane patches.

claim: The β-turn is required very early in assembly, perhaps during nucleation of the viral particle.
source: On the other hand, the β-turn is required very early in assembly, perhaps during nucleation of the viral particle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that β-turn mutants fail to form membrane patches.

claim: In context of full-length HIV-1 Gag, the entire CA-SP1 switch region was suggested to be unstructured but with weak helical propensity.
source: In context of full-length HIV-1 Gag, the entire CA-SP1 switch region was suggested to be unstructured but with weak helical propensity (Newman et al., 2004; Worthylake et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous NMR studies.

claim: A fully folded β-turn (but not junction helix) was observed in the crystal structure of the immature-like dimer form of the CTD.
source: A fully folded β-turn (but not junction helix) was also observed in the crystal structure of the immature-like dimer form of the CTD (Bartonova et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous crystal structure.

claim: In the unassembled, soluble Gag protein, the β-turn fluctuates between folded and unfolded states, and the entire CA-SP1 junction folds only upon assembly of the immature lattice.
source: We therefore speculate that in the unassembled, soluble Gag protein, the β-turn fluctuates between folded and unfolded states, and that the entire CA-SP1 junction folds only upon assembly of the immature lattice.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: Folding of the CA-SP1 switch, and in particular the β-turn, is a critical step in nucleation of the immature Gag lattice.
source: Since we found that an intact β-turn sequence cannot rescue a defective junction helix and vice versa (at least in vitro), we propose that folding of the CA-SP1 switch, and in particular the β-turn, is a critical step in nucleation of the immature Gag lattice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mutagenesis data.

claim: Assembly of retroviral particles is thought to initiate when the viral RNA genome dimerizes and exposes high-affinity binding sites for the Gag C-terminal NC domain.
source: Assembly of retroviral particles is thought to initiate when the viral RNA genome dimerizes and exposes high-affinity binding sites for the Gag C-terminal NC domain (D'Souza and Summers, 2004; Keane et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The resulting ribonucleoprotein complex, containing several Gag molecules, is reasonably assumed to nucleate assembly of the immature viral particle.
source: The resulting ribonucleoprotein complex, containing several Gag molecules, is reasonably assumed to nucleate assembly of the immature viral particle.
evidence: This is a reasonable assumption based on established knowledge.

claim: RNA-mediated Gag clustering has been proposed to nucleate assembly by promoting the CTD dimerization interaction.
source: RNA-mediated Gag clustering has been proposed to nucleate assembly by promoting the CTD dimerization interaction (Amarasinghe et al., 2000; Bush and Vogt, 2014; Ma and Vogt, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RNA-mediated clustering directly promotes folding of the CA-SP1 junction and the 6-helix bundle and, thereby, formation of Gag hexamers.
source: Since the isolated SP1 peptide folds into a helix in a concentration dependent manner (Datta et al., 2011), we suggest instead that RNA-mediated clustering directly promotes folding of the CA-SP1 junction and the 6-helix bundle and, thereby, formation of Gag hexamers.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from cited data and the current structural findings.

claim: A hexamer is more intuitively appealing as the nucleator of the spherical Gag shell than a dimer, since it is the smallest unit comprising the set of protein-protein interactions that are exclusive to the immature lattice.
source: Compared to a dimer, a hexamer is more intuitively appealing as the nucleator of the spherical Gag shell, since it is the smallest unit comprising the set of protein-protein interactions that are exclusive to the immature lattice and not found in the mature capsid or other functional states of the protein.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on structural analysis.

claim: Folding of the junction will have the additional role of reeling in the NC domain and its bound genome, increasing the probability that the accumulating Gag molecules will bind to the same RNA.
source: We further speculate that folding of the junction will have the additional role of reeling in the NC domain and its bound genome, increasing the probability that the accumulating Gag molecules will bind to the same RNA.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the structural model.

claim: The RNA exerts some corresponding pulling force on the assembling Gag lattice, helping to promote its encapsidation.
source: It is likely that the RNA, in turn, exerts some corresponding pulling force on the assembling Gag lattice, helping to promote its encapsidation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference.

claim: The CA-SP1 junction allosterically communicates the status of downstream NC/RNA events to the upstream assembly domains of Gag.
source: Our analysis therefore supports the proposal that the CA-SP1 junction allosterically communicates the status of downstream NC/RNA events to the upstream assembly domains of Gag (Bush and Vogt, 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural and functional data, and supported by citation.

claim: Retroviruses that do not contain a spacer between their CA and NC domains might have eschewed sophisticated protease regulation but have retained the more fundamental assembly determinant at the C-terminal end of CA.
source: Retroviruses that do not contain a spacer between their CA and NC domains might have eschewed sophisticated protease regulation but have retained the more fundamental assembly determinant at the C-terminal end of CA.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the structural findings.

claim: MPMV does not have a spacer element, but does appear to have a 'clasp' motif that is similar to that of HIV-1.
source: Sequence comparison confirms that MPMV does not have a spacer element, but does appear to have a 'clasp' motif that is similar to that of HIV-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MPMV's immature capsid structure does not contain a 6-helix bundle.
source: An example is Mason-Pfizer monkey virus (MPMV), whose immature capsid structure does not contain a 6-helix bundle (Bharat et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claim: RSV has a well-characterized spacer but does not have a recognizable turn motif.
source: Rous sarcoma virus (RSV) appears to be a contrasting example – it has a well-characterized spacer (Bush et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2008; Schur et al., 2015a), but does not have a recognizable turn motif.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The RSV junction helix is longer and more stable than that of HIV-1.
source: The RSV junction helix is longer and more stable than that of HIV-1 (Bush et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2008), and we surmise that the RSV spacer confers both the assembly and regulatory functions that are mediated by two distinct parts in HIV.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The RSV spacer confers both the assembly and regulatory functions that are mediated by two distinct parts in HIV.
source: The RSV junction helix is longer and more stable than that of HIV-1 (Bush et al., 2014; Keller et al., 2008), and we surmise that the RSV spacer confers both the assembly and regulatory functions that are mediated by two distinct parts in HIV.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from comparative analysis.

claim: Schur et al. report a cryoEM structure of the immature HIV-1 Gag lattice at near-atomic resolution in a concurrent publication.
source: In a concurrent publication, Schur et al. report a cryoEM structure of the immature HIV-1 Gag lattice at near-atomic resolution (Schur et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a concurrent publication.

claim: Schur et al. also conclude that the CA-SP1 boundary folds into a 6-helix bundle that is important for assembly of Gag and its proteolytic maturation.
source: They also conclude that the CA-SP1 boundary folds into a 6-helix bundle that is important for assembly of Gag and its proteolytic maturation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a concurrent publication.

claim: The CTD-SP1 construct used in these studies contained the P373T substitution, which is a natural sequence variant.
source: The construct also contained the P373T substitution, which is a natural sequence variant (Kuiken et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a sequence database.

claim: The diffraction data were weak (mean I/σ<I> = 6 and completeness = 87%) due to the small size of the crystal (~20 microns in the longest dimension).
source: Due to the small size of the crystal (~20 microns in the longest dimension), the diffraction data were weak (mean I/σ<I> = 6 and completeness = 87%; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: Very high quality maps for model building were obtained due to the fortuitous existence of 6-fold non-crystallographic symmetry (NCS), and through the use of modern density modification techniques implemented in PHENIX.
source: Nevertheless, we obtained very high quality maps for model building due to the fortuitous existence of 6-fold non-crystallographic symmetry (NCS), and through the use of modern density modification techniques implemented in PHENIX.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystallographic methods and results.

claim: The immature △MA-CA-SP1-NC VLPs are nearly identical to the immature Gag shell of authentic virions.
source: The immature △MA-CA-SP1-NC VLPs are nearly identical to the immature Gag shell of authentic virions (Briggs et al., 2009; Gross et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.
